questions.q: What role does Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD) play in the record-access stack, per this lesson?
options: It's an optional setting most orgs skip
It's the baseline floor -- every other mechanism only ever widens what OWD allows, never narrows it
It's the final, most restrictive check applied after everything else
It only applies to custom objects, never standard ones
questions.explain: OWD sets the baseline record access, and sharing rules, role hierarchy, and manual sharing can only widen it from there.

questions.q: What does Public Read Only grant, per this lesson?
options: Only the record owner can view or edit it
Everyone in the org can view the record; only the owner and role hierarchy can edit it
Everyone can view and edit the record
No one can view the record except System Administrators
questions.explain: Public Read Only lets everyone view, but edit stays restricted to the owner and those above them in the role hierarchy.

questions.q: Why does an object's OWD have separate Internal and External Access columns?
options: External access can never be more permissive than internal access
They're identical settings duplicated for no reason
Internal access only applies to API integrations
External access always overrides internal access
questions.explain: The lesson explains external (portal/community/guest) access can never exceed internal (employee) access for the same object.

questions.q: In the lesson's three-question decision framework, what determines whether an object's OWD should be Private?
options: Whether the object has more than 10,000 records
Whether there will ever be an instance of the object the most restricted user shouldn't be allowed to see
Whether the object is standard or custom
Whether the object has a Lookup relationship to Account
questions.explain: If the most restricted user who needs the object at all should never see every instance of it, the answer is Private.

questions.q: Per this lesson, can a sharing rule or the role hierarchy ever grant a user less access than an object's OWD allows?
options: Yes, sharing rules can override OWD downward in some cases
No -- every mechanism above OWD in the stack only widens access, never narrows it
Yes, if the role hierarchy is disabled
It depends on whether the object is Private or Public
questions.explain: The lesson states OWD is the floor; nothing above it in the stack can reduce access below what OWD already grants.
